statement: Background checks required before a person joins are defined, such as identity, references, qualifications and criminal record where lawful, with depth scaled to the role, the information it can reach and the risk. The checks are completed before the start date or before access is granted. The procedure states when re-screening happens, for example on promotion to a sensitive role. Screening records prove it.
why_asked: Unchecked hires in sensitive roles are a common route to insider incidents and fraud.
how_to_ask: Ask for the screening procedure and for the records of recent joiners. Example probe: "For the last administrator you hired, show me which checks were done and when, relative to their first day."
question: Does your organization check the background of candidates before they join, in proportion to the risk of the role?
expected_evidence: Screening procedure; screening records for joiners; re-screening records or triggers. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: The procedure sets checks by role risk and notes lawful limits. Records show checks done before start or access. Re-screening triggers are defined and applied.
test: Sample joiners in the period, weighted toward sensitive roles. Pass if each sampled joiner has the required checks recorded as complete before the start date or before access was granted, and the procedure states when re-screening occurs.
baseline_risk: Untrustworthy or unqualified people gain access to sensitive information.

statement: Employment and contractor agreement templates state the security responsibilities of both the individual and the organization. All current staff and contractors sign agreements that contain these terms, and the signed copies are kept. This makes security duties part of the working relationship and gives a basis for action if they are breached.
why_asked: Duties that are not in the contract are hard to enforce and easy to overlook.
how_to_ask: Ask for the contract templates and a few signed contracts. Example probe: "Show me the clause where a contractor accepts responsibility for protecting company information."
question: Does your organization state security responsibilities in signed agreements with staff?
expected_evidence: Employment and contractor agreement templates; sample of signed agreements for current staff and contractors. Cover the current workforce.
good_looks_like: Templates carry security responsibilities for individual and organization. Signed copies exist for current staff and contractors.
test: Sample current staff and contractors. Pass if the templates contain the security terms and every sampled signed agreement includes them.
baseline_risk: Staff and contractors may not be bound by clear security duties.

statement: A security awareness program is delivered to all personnel and relevant outside parties. It covers the security policy, each person's contribution and the consequences of non-compliance. It also covers common threats such as phishing and malicious attachments. Personnel complete it within the period the program sets, non-completers are followed up, and people are updated whenever relevant policies or procedures change. Completion reports prove it.
why_asked: People are the most targeted entry point, and awareness that is not tracked or refreshed fades quickly.
how_to_ask: Ask for the program, the completion report and the latest policy-change communication. Example probe: "Who has not completed training this cycle, and what happens to them?"
question: Does your organization keep all personnel aware of their security responsibilities?
expected_evidence: Awareness program with content, audience and cycle; completion report with follow-up of non-completers; phishing and malware awareness material; communications about policy changes. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: A program defines content, audience and cycle. Nearly all in-scope people complete it on time, and non-completers are chased. Policy changes are communicated, and phishing content was delivered.
test: Take the in-scope population list and sample people. Pass if the program is defined, each sampled person has a completion record inside the defined period or a tracked follow-up, malware awareness material was delivered in the period, and at least one policy change was communicated.
baseline_risk: People fall for common attacks and do not know what the organization expects of them.

statement: People in technical, privileged and other high-risk roles receive training matched to their duties, such as secure coding for developers. A role-based curriculum is defined, completion is tracked, and it is refreshed at least yearly for developers. Training records prove it.
why_asked: General awareness does not give administrators and developers the skills their work demands, and mistakes in these roles do more damage.
how_to_ask: Ask which roles need specific training and for the completion records. Example probe: "When did your developers last take secure coding training, and who has not?"
question: Does your organization give people in technical, privileged and other high-risk roles training matched to their duties?
expected_evidence: Role-based training curriculum; list of technical, privileged and high-risk roles; completion records, including secure coding training for developers. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: High-risk roles are listed, each has defined training, and completion is tracked. Developers have taken secure coding training in the last year.
test: Sample people in technical, privileged and developer roles. Pass if each sampled person has a completion record for the training defined for their role, and each sampled developer completed secure coding training within the last year.
baseline_risk: Privileged and technical staff lack the skills to avoid or spot role-specific security mistakes.
applicability: The secure coding element applies if the organization develops software in house.
key_settings: base: developer secure coding training: at least once a year

statement: The competence needed by people whose work affects security performance is determined, and those people are shown to have it, through education, training or experience. Where competence is missing, action is taken to gain it and checked to see whether it worked. Evidence of competence is kept on file and reviewed on a defined cycle.
why_asked: A security program run by people without the right skills tends to fail quietly.
how_to_ask: Ask which roles affect security performance, what competence each needs, and how gaps are closed. Example probe: "Pick one security role and show me how you know the person holds the skills it needs."
question: Does your organization make sure the people who affect security performance have the competence their roles need?
expected_evidence: Competence requirements for security-relevant roles; qualification, training or experience records; action plans for competence gaps and their evaluation. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Required competence is written per role. Records show each holder meets it, and gaps have an action and a later check.
test: Sample holders of security-relevant roles. Pass if each has competence records matching the written requirement, and any gap has a recorded action and an evaluation of the result.
baseline_risk: People may run security work without the skills to do it well.

statement: A documented disciplinary process covers violations of security policy and is communicated to all personnel, for example through the handbook, policy acknowledgement or training. When a violation occurs, the process is applied and the outcome is recorded. This gives people a clear understanding of the consequences and the organization a fair way to act.
why_asked: Without a known disciplinary route, security rules lack consequences and responses vary from case to case.
how_to_ask: Ask for the process, how people learn about it, and how recent violations were handled. Example probe: "How would a staff member learn that sharing a password can lead to formal action?"
question: Does your organization have a formal, communicated disciplinary process for security policy violations?
expected_evidence: Disciplinary procedure that covers security violations; handbook, policy acknowledgement or training content that communicates it; records of cases handled. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: A written process covers security violations. Personnel receive it at joining and when it changes. Cases follow the process and are recorded.
test: Review the procedure, then sample personnel and any cases in the period. Pass if the procedure covers security violations, each sampled person has evidence of receiving it, and each sampled case followed the procedure.
baseline_risk: Security policy breaches have no agreed consequences, which weakens compliance.

statement: The security responsibilities that continue after employment ends or changes, such as confidentiality and return of information, are defined and stated in contracts or leaver documents. At exit, these obligations are communicated to each leaver, and an exit letter or signed acknowledgement is kept. This keeps former staff bound after they stop having access.
why_asked: People who leave still know company secrets, and obligations that are not repeated at exit are easy to dismiss.
how_to_ask: Ask for the contract clause or exit document and the records for recent leavers. Example probe: "What do you give a departing engineer that reminds them what they must still protect?"
question: Does your organization define and communicate the security duties that continue after a person leaves or changes role?
expected_evidence: Contract templates or leaver documents that state continuing duties; exit letters or signed acknowledgements for leavers. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Continuing duties are written down and are part of the exit steps. Every leaver has a record that they were told.
test: Sample leavers and role changes in the period. Pass if each sampled person has an exit letter or acknowledgement, and the continuing duties appear in the contract or leaver document.
baseline_risk: Former staff may reuse or share information because nobody reminded them of their duties.

statement: Confidentiality agreement templates for staff and for relevant external parties are kept and reflect the organization's protection needs. Staff, contractors and external parties with access sign them before access begins, and the templates are reviewed on a defined cycle. Signed copies and template version history prove it.
why_asked: Without signed confidentiality terms, disclosure of sensitive information is harder to prevent or challenge.
how_to_ask: Ask for the templates and a few signed agreements. Example probe: "Which agreement did the last external consultant sign before seeing client data and when was that template last reviewed?"
question: Does your organization have staff and relevant external parties sign confidentiality agreements that reflect its protection needs?
expected_evidence: Confidentiality agreement templates for staff and external parties; signed agreements for a sample of staff, contractors and external parties; template version history and review record. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Templates fit the information being protected. Everyone with access to confidential information has signed before access. Templates are reviewed on the defined cycle and changes are tracked.
test: Sample staff, contractors and external parties with access to confidential information. Pass if each has a signed agreement on file dated no later than their access, and the template history shows a review within the defined cycle.
baseline_risk: Confidential information can be disclosed with no enforceable obligation.
